title: Is there life elsewhere in the Universe?
subtitle: Exobiology
subject: sciences
description: Trillions of planets, and yet total radio silence. Science looks for life elsewhere without promising little green men.

hero.hook: The universe is enormous. So why is nobody answering?

blocks.text: The observable universe holds about **2 trillion** galaxies, vast gatherings of stars, each one with hundreds of billions of stars. On the numbers alone, potentially habitable planets should be beyond counting. Yet since modern astronomy began, we have not had a single confirmed contact.

This contradiction has a name: the **Fermi paradox**, after the physicist **Enrico Fermi**. The question is no longer only science fiction. It belongs to [[Exobiology]], the science of how life might appear elsewhere and how we could detect it.

Any search starts from the only example we know: life on Earth. It rests above all on the chemistry of **carbon**, an atom that builds complex molecules, and on **liquid water**, which lets chemical reactions run smoothly.

blocks.caption: Radio telescopes scan the sky, listening for a possible signal

blocks.text: A candidate planet usually has to sit in its star's [[habitable zone]]: not too close, or the water boils away, and not too far, or it freezes. Since the 1990s we have found more than **5,500 exoplanets**, planets orbiting stars other than the Sun. Almost every star in our galaxy is thought to have at least one.
There are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.

In **1961**, the astronomer **Frank Drake** proposed the [[Drake equation]]: a formula that multiplies a string of factors (stars, habitable planets, how long civilizations last) to estimate how many communicating civilizations the Milky Way holds. The numbers are still very uncertain. The formula mainly serves to give the debate a structure.

There is no need to head for other stars just yet. Several worlds in our own solar system are intriguing. **Europa**, a moon of Jupiter, probably holds an ocean of liquid water under a crust of ice. That ocean most likely stays liquid thanks to [[tidal forces]]: the huge pull of Jupiter stretches Europa and heats its interior by friction.

**Enceladus**, a small moon of Saturn, throws out **geysers**, jets of vapor and matter. The **Cassini** probe found signs of **hydrothermal** activity there, heat from chemical reactions on the ocean floor, which could in principle feed microbes with no sunlight at all.

On **Mars**, liquid water once ran across the surface. Rovers there hunt for [[biosignatures]]: fossil or chemical traces of past life, from before the planet lost most of its atmosphere and its water.

In **1950**, Fermi asked the blunt question: if advanced civilizations exist by the thousand, why do we see no trace of them? The universe is old. A civilization only a million years ahead of us would have had time to make itself noticed, even without traveling at the speed of light.

One answer is the [[Great Filter]]: a step in evolution that is almost impossible to pass, such as the jump to complex life, or technological self-destruction. Either we are already through it, or it still lies ahead of us.

Other leads: perhaps we are listening for the wrong signals. The **SETI** program, Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, scans radio waves above all. Perhaps civilizations are too short-lived and too far apart to ever overlap. Or perhaps the [[zoo hypothesis]] is right: Earth is being left alone on purpose, like a nature reserve.

The **James Webb** Space Telescope studies the light that passes through the atmosphere of distant planets, using [[spectroscopy]], the splitting of light to identify which gases are present. Astronomers look for gases such as oxygen or methane in strange amounts, a possible hint of life.
If someone in the Andromeda galaxy were watching us “now,” they would see the Earth as it was **2.5 million years** ago: that is how long the light takes to make the trip.

Even microbial life would change everything: it would prove that life is not a one-off accident. In the meantime, the **Voyager** probes have carried gold records of Earth's sounds and images since **1977**. Odds of interception: almost zero. Our need not to feel alone: as strong as ever.
Planets are beyond counting and life looks statistically plausible. But the silence, the Fermi paradox, is a reminder that technological intelligence may be very rare, or very brief.
